en: The Lamp for the Integration of Practices.
Chapter One. Om, homage to Śrī Vajrasattva!
Bow to the one who is space-like, devoid of intrinsic nature, and pure; bow to the one who is without remainder, beyond syllables, and inexpressible.
Bow to the Sugata who has gone everywhere in the future; bow to the one who is entirely and completely empty of all things.
"One should rely on the meaning, but the words may be as they are. Thus it is said in the *Tantra*:
"In the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma of the Great Sage..."
"Indeed, all those who do not know reality are truly without fruit.
Therefore, it is said:
"The connection for beginners is for the purpose of leading them into the ultimate truth."
"And indeed, the skillful means have been fashioned by the Perfectly Awakened Ones like a staircase.
Thus ends the first chapter, "The Melāvaṇa for Awakening: The Resolution of Doubts. 1.
2. Second Chapter:
The five aggregates are briefly proclaimed as the five Buddhas;
the vajra sense-bases themselves are the supreme maṇḍala of the Bodhisattvas.
The earth element is known as Locanā; the water element is remembered as Māmakī;
that which is called Pāṇḍarā is fire; and Tārā is proclaimed to be wind.
The mantra-practitioner should always meditate upon the deity by means of forms, sounds, and so forth.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One in the Śrī-Guhyasamāja Mahāyoga Tantra:
"Families are said to be of a hundred kinds, yet in brief they are fivefold;
furthermore, they come to be threefold through the division of body, speech, and mind."
“The five aggregates are briefly proclaimed as the five Buddhas;
resting upon the five hearts, they emerge from the five bodies, are conjoined with the five winds, and effect the enjoyment of the five desires. Thus it is said.

Because it moves forth through the doors of the senses by means of the threads [of the vital breath], and because it constantly proceeds through the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), it is designated as "prāṇa."
Because it carries away wind, urine, feces, as well as semen and the like,
this is always perceived by yogis as the apāna.
That which constantly brings together everything that is eaten, chewed, licked, drunk, and sucked is called the *samāna* [wind].
Because it moves upward, because it withdraws [the breath], and because it consumes food, drink, and so forth,
this udāna is known through its association with knowledge as the activity of the vital energy.
Because it pervades all the joints and performs functions such as holding, moving, and returning, it is called vyāna.
The earth element is known as Locanā; the water element is remembered as Māmakī;
fire is known as Pāṇḍarā; and wind is proclaimed as Tārā.
The aggregates, the elements, and likewise the sense faculties—each set being fivefold—are differentiated in this very way.
Sustained by the empowerment of the Tathāgata, how could the karmas of saṃsāra arise from each one individually?
Likewise, the five external objects, each individually, are eternally presided over by the five Tathāgatas; they are supported by the three gnoses and the five [skandhas].

"One should contemplate the mandala born of all vajras situated in the center of the element-space; and one should perform the withdrawal if one desires to hold the peaceful vajra. Thus it is said. The body of humans is seen to consist of five, being composed of the five elements themselves.
"By cultivating their own minds through the presence or absence of those [states], the Buddhas manifest. Thus it is said; and in the *Khasamatantra* it is also stated:
"Behold this entire world as the nature of the five Buddhas, like a divine and variegated drama."
For in this [state], one dances as the Great Friend, while another [dances] with manifold passion.
"In brief, however, it is fivefold":
through the contemplations of body, speech, and mind, no intrinsic nature is apprehended.
Through the application of the mantra-form, there is neither awakening nor meditative cultivation.

"Having briefly reflected upon this characteristic of body, speech, and mind, one should cultivate the meditative absorption (samādhi) fashioned by mantra, which is the union with the ritual procedure. Thus,
yoga does not arise in reflections [or images] such as those cast in metal and so forth.
Therefore, for the yogi of the great yoga of bodhicitta, all deities [are one].
"The self indeed is all-buddhahood and the very sovereignty over sentient beings;
therefore, through the yoga of one's own presiding deity, one should accomplish the self alone. Thus it is said.
Impelled by body, speech, and mind through the contemplation of the mantra,
one should accomplish the supreme siddhi, which is dear because it satisfies the mind.
The second [chapter], the resolution of doubts concerning physical seclusion and the gathering [of practitioners]. // 2 //
3. The third chapter:
"One should always meditate with effort through yoga upon a great five-colored jewel, the size of a mustard seed, at the tip of the nose. Thus it is said.
The breath consists of the five wisdoms and has the nature of the five elements.
Having expelled [the breath], one should imagine it in the form of a single mass at the tip of the lotus-nose;
this great jewel of five colors is known as *prāṇāyāma*.
Then the Blessed One, the Great Vajrin, the teacher of the world, having been properly prostrated to by him who speaks the purpose of vajra-recitation, replied to him alone.
This very mind of awakening (bodhicitta) has been revealed as the worldly scripture itself.
How indeed will future generations understand that which is supramundane?
For you have taught the Dharma for the sake of abandoning all views;
how then has that very view, the thought of enlightenment, been made so firm?
Deluded by the words of the twilight [teachings], they do not understand the meaning that has been spoken;
they grasp it according to the literal sound and indeed digest it in that very same way.
Then the Blessed One Viśva said to Vajrapāṇi:
"Excellent, excellent, O Lord of Secrets! You have prophesied the future."
The bodhicitta becomes the wind, established in the sky;
it is the vital breath of sentient beings, consisting of five aspects and known by ten names.
The threefold nature [of the body] arises from its own-being as that which is called the twelve-linked dependent origination;
this, the foremost of all the sense faculties, is known as wind and is the bodhicitta.
That which is unmanifest is always described as subtle, yet it is called manifest;
depending upon that, people perform actions such as those directed toward sense objects.
Pacification, enrichment, as well as subjugation and the rite of sorcery—
all these arise from the thought of awakening, which is the locus and support of the three principles.
Just as various conventional signs of light are imagined,
so too do conceptual constructions always arise from the wind-like mind of awakening.
Phenomena such as pleasure and pain are produced from the seed alone;
this has the nature of bodhicitta and is like the non-duality of the aggregates and so forth.
Through the single union of wisdom and means, the world shall become the awakened mind.
The master himself should recite it, setting aside meditation and study.
Through the division of day and night and by means of the moon and sun,
the breath— which pervades the world— is indeed the single wind of the bodhicitta.
"Having abandoned the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious, one indeed becomes like the sky. [Thus it is said.
[One should master] those known as prāṇa, apāna, and samāna, as well as those designated as udāna and vyāna, and [the five winds] Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.
"Having thus fashioned their own images and emanated the female principle (strītattva),
they [became] Koṭākṣa, Koṭava, Koṭa, Koṭābha,
and Koṭīraka; as well as Kolākṣa, Kolāva, Kola, Kolābha, and Kali."
Arising from the nostrils and abiding within the five Buddha families,
the five winds move upward and circulate perpetually within the body.
Emerging from the gateway of the movement of the concealed nose, these are of four kinds: those moving through the left, the right, both together, and the motionless.
The expansion from the south is the element of fire and indeed the mandala of the consumer of oblations;
this red-colored face of Padmanātha should be visualized as moving forth.
From the left, the flow of the element emerges from the wind-maṇḍala;
greenish-black in appearance, it moves as the lord of karma.
The flow of the *dvandva* is the element of Kanakavarṇa together with the three;
and the mandala of Māhendra moves as that of Ratnanātha.
Stable and without expansion, the element becomes in an instant the mandala of Varuṇa;
resembling pure crystal, it moves within the Lord of Vajra.
Having extracted the entire realm, supported by the relationship of the container and the contained,
the great body of Vairocana shall emerge at the end of death.
One should indeed recite this fourfold mandala daily with a concentrated mind;
for practitioners of mantra, the recitation should always continue day and night according to the prescribed number of recitations.
One who is not bound by the ten [qualities] among those beginning with one and ending with nine—one should know him to be unbound; he knows the supreme state.
He who knows the vowels and consonants, following the number nine, and whose mutual conjunctions are unbound, is the Guru of the world.
Whoever,
having heard this, should desire accomplishment— the perfection of the fruit of liberation—
attains that very state, formless and devoid of material form.
Joined with the end of the elements (bhūtānta), it resides in the sixteenth digit (kalā) and so forth;
it is conjoined with five pentads and arranged in four triads.
Accompanied by the anusvāra and long vowels, and characterized by the combination and elision of phonemes (guṇa and saṃyoga), the entire sentence would be short; it is neither manifold nor singular.
Whatever is to be accomplished by one desiring success must be done with the meaning of the letter *ya*;
indeed, the activity of the world proceeds through the triad beginning with the letter *ra*.
Those phonemes which were previously described as being behind, as well as those which face forward,
are female, male, and neuter, and are conceived as belonging to the [three] elements and so forth.
Then, having understood through the intellect those [vowels] joined vertically and those applied horizontally,
one realizes that which is spoken of by the six, the four, the three, and the one, as being born from the single nature of the absence of intrinsic existence.
Having applied [the mantra] for the sake of protection and other purposes, the knowledge of the three times arises;
having destroyed [ignorance] like a dream or a magical illusion, one should act within the triple world.
This mantra of withdrawal arises from the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature;
from that, the transformed form emerges which brings about the perception of the deity.
This supreme *bodhicitta* is conventional, established within the three principles (*tritattva*), characterized by the recitation of *prakṛti*, ineffable, and beyond utterance.
That very triad becomes one, without departure and without arrival,
without cessation, perfectly tranquil, and free from eternalism and nihilism.
This is the ultimate reality itself, characterized by being personally realized within, marked by non-differentiation from space, and having formed its resolve throughout the three times.
In all activities,
including sitting and so forth,
the knower of yoga should always recite that which is inexpressible, unutterable, and transcendent of the three times.
The recitation (japa) of Pāṇḍarā and the others is said to be two hundred and twenty-five;
when correctly multiplied by four, it is nine hundred and sixteen.
That which was observed as nine hundred [breaths] in twenty-four circumambulations would,
from the moment of commencement, become twenty-two hundred and sixteen.
Thus, in this way, the subtle yoga has been revealed in the Guhyasandhyā;
nevertheless, even though it is free from meditation and recitation, it is called "japa."
"The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, the supreme syllable;
it is indeed the Great Breath, unarisen, and devoid of verbal expression.
It is the foremost cause of all speech and is the perfect radiance of all words. Thus [it is said].
"Burning like a lamp, in the center of the heart is the unstruck (*anāhata*);
it is the imperishable, supreme, subtle *akāra*, the supreme Lord. Thus, these phenomena are explained by means of the sound of words.

"For neither 'dharma' nor 'sound' is found here; and by not descending into the state of oneness, one will touch the unsurpassed, supreme patience which is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Thus it is said.
The third [chapter], the determination of doubts concerning the isolation and union of speech, is concluded. // 3 //
4. The Fourth Chapter:
"Those who settle the mind—which wanders far, moves alone, is bodiless, and dwells in the cave—are liberated from the bonds of Māra. Thus it is said.
Whatever arises dependently through the sense faculties, their objects, and the mind.
"Because it protects by means of the eighty-fold manifestation known as *tanmanas*, [it is called *tāntrika*].
Knowledge consists of pure consciousness alone, being without defining characteristics like space;
however, it possesses a differentiation consisting of the forms of twilight, night, and day.
Light, the radiance of light, and likewise the perception of light—mind is said to be threefold; its support is now described.
Through the subtle form of the vital air, consciousness has attained a state of complete integration.
Having emerged from the pathways of the sense faculties, it does not take objects as its support.
When the wind, joined with the manifestation, becomes the vehicle,
then its entire nature proceeds in both an orderly and a disordered manner.
"Wherever the wind is situated, it carries that very same nature.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Melāpaṇa of Doubt regarding the Isolation of the Mind. 4.
5. The fifth chapter:
Just as many clouds, possessing various shapes and colors, arise from the expanse of the sky and indeed dissolve back into it; so too [is the nature of all things].
All these natures, having the three appearances as their cause,
enter the clear light after having experienced all objects.
Having such a nature, veiled by the cataracts of ignorance regarding consciousness, they perform virtuous and non-virtuous actions and wander through the five realms of existence.
Having committed an act of immediate retribution or the like, one ripens in the hells;
having performed virtuous acts such as giving, one is honored in the heavens and other realms.
Having thus experienced this again and again throughout thousands of endless births,
one grieves out of delusion, thinking, "This is the ripening of my past karma."
"Those people who possess afflictions through the process of the manifestation of intrinsic nature—having understood this, the wise are liberated from the cage of existence. Thus it is said.
If all this is empty and devoid of an unarisen intrinsic nature, [how can there be bondage?]"
How does karma function here in this saṃsāra to produce pleasure and pain?
Through the notions of "I" and "mine," as well as the impurities such as passion and the like,
fools— imagining [these] by means of the dependent nature— are afflicted by suffering.
"All this is mind-only, arising like a magical illusion;
from that comes virtuous and non-virtuous karma, and from that comes virtuous and non-virtuous birth.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the "Resolution of Doubts Concerning the Distinction and Integration of Karma."
6. The Sixth Chapter:
"Through the cultivation of reality, one obtains a body resembling a rainbow. Thus it is said.
When one abides in equanimity toward the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, faculties, and so forth, as well as within those two types of knowledge;
When there is emptiness and a state of great magnitude, he who is asleep indeed beholds a dream due to the force of the wind.
One who desires the fruits of a dream should not conceive of any difference between dreaming and waking;
for a living being, having slept for a very long time in the state of solid earth, undergoes the dream throughout day and night.
When the fruit is not yet ripe and the deeds have been performed, the vital breath (vāyu) moves again toward birth in this world;
when the fruit is ripe, the breath has already departed, for death comes swiftly in the next world.
Just as the Lord of Jinas, though established in the ten directions, has no marrow, bone, or flesh in his body,
yet for the benefit of sentient beings, he performs his deeds through the manifestation of relics as if by magical transformation.
Thus, in due course, one who is awake yet has a sleeping mind desires the fruit within the web of conceptual construction.

Indeed, all phenomena are like a dream; they are neither false nor true, for there is the absence of both. Thus ends the sixth chapter, the "Elimination of Doubts," concerning the blending of conventional truth. 6.
7. The Seventh Chapter:
Just as a lamp situated inside a jar does not illuminate what is outside, but after that jar is broken, the flame of the lamp shines forth; so it is with the self.
For one's own body is indeed the jar, and the lamp is indeed the reality;
when these are joined by the mouth of the Guru, the wisdom of the Buddha becomes manifest.
"He sees the sky as arisen from the sky, the space of space;
for in this very way, this practice has been demonstrated from the mouth of the Guru.
Thus, these phenomena are explained by means of vocal sounds, yet neither phenomenon nor sound is found here.
"And having entered into the oneness of the unsurpassed nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one will touch the supreme patience.
Homage to you, O best of Vajras, granter of boons; homage be to you, O limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)! Homage to you, whose womb is emptiness; homage be to you, O awakening of the Buddhas!
O Great Teacher, grant me the vision of perfect awakening—
the supreme, universal emptiness that is the great primordial wisdom of all Buddhas.
"O Mahāsattva, grant me that which is characterized solely by your own power;
may I attain awakening right here, liberated from karma and birth."
O Lord, apart from Your lotus feet, there is no other refuge;
therefore, be gracious, O foremost of Buddhas, O hero of the world, O great sage!
Having thus offered that supreme rite of divine supplication,
the illustrious Guru, an ocean of virtues, having generated compassion for the disciple, [proceeded].
Having become serene of face, compassionate, and joyful,
he should cause [the disciple] to hear the supreme, divine samaya arising from the Yoga-tantra.
Then the preceptor, being composed in meditation, should generate the thought of awakening;
having placed the thought of awakening either in a flask or in a conch shell.
Then, having summoned that disciple who has been empowered by all the Buddhas,
he should entrust him with the samaya, accompanied by the mudrā of the Jina.
Indeed, the consecration must be bestowed by the second Vajrī himself,
accompanied by auspicious and non-malicious sounds and the various melodies of musical instruments.
Having performed the consecration of the three realms, the disciple, with palms joined in reverence, should then be granted permission by the preceptor, being urged therein.
The garland, the water, the awakened vajra and bell, and then the mirror; the naming, the master [initiation], and the authorization—this indeed is the sequence of the consecrations.
Then one should transmit to him the characteristic of external awakening—that which has been obtained in the tradition and has come down through the succession of gurus. Thus:
"The drop that is dissolved in pure water, whether in a river or a lake..."
The yogi should constantly remember that pure [state] as it is described through the successive stages of penetration;

for just as the cessation of the wind is not perceived when it has reached its end within a mirror, so too the grasping of a solid body is no longer seen— thus is the sequence envisioned by those who possess the prescribed method.
Transcending the cultivation of all limbs, free from conceptual construction and its fabrications, and surpassing both the measures and the bindu— this is the supreme maṇḍala.
That which enters into all states of being, whether with form or formless, is the stainless mind—
awakened and impelled— which is the mandala, having the nature of a mandala.
"It exists" and "it does not exist"—both are extremes; "purity" and "impurity"—these too are extremes.
Therefore, having avoided both extremes, the wise person does not take a stand even in the middle.
Thus, it is for the sake of the infinity of space, the great abode of all beings.
The sovereign Lord Śrī is the manifestation of power, the king who fulfills all hopes.
Oho, Buddha! Oho, Buddha! Oho, the teaching of the Dharma!
O you whose purpose is the purity of the meaning of pure reality, to your bodhicitta, homage be paid!
The seventh [chapter], the resolution of doubts concerning the distillation of ultimate truth. // 7 //
8. The eighth chapter:
"They say that the gross consists of sound, and likewise the subtle consists of mind;
that which is devoid of mind is the supreme state of yogins. Thus it is said.
That reality is to be personally realized; it cannot be described to another. It is accessible through the cultivation of devotion, but otherwise it is not accessible at all.
Having realized the truth and then cultivated a state of devotion day and night,
[one abides] in that supreme state of Nirvana, which is peaceful and unsurpassed.
Then, through the power of devotion to that [deity] and produced by the force of meditative cultivation,
there arises within him a certain supreme form born of bliss.
Arising with the form of the syllable *dhag*, it manifests as a process of expansion and withdrawal,
illuminating all this— *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, and *svar*— along with everything moving and stationary.
Through the power and efficacy of meditative cultivation, one attains the auspicious state consisting of wisdom and skillful means,
which is completely liberated from all afflictions and adorned with all the [auspicious] marks.
Born from the knowledge of emptiness, it is beyond duality, supremely auspicious,
endowed with the excellence of all aspects, and free from the subject-object dichotomy.
Knowledge is like an illusion—pure, transparent, and naturally stainless;
it transcends sound, smell, and taste, and is likewise devoid of touch.
In the supreme meditative absorption, one perceives with the eye of wisdom that which is divine,
resembling a shadow or an illusion, and endowed with divine forms.
Those who contemplate reality attain a body resembling a rainbow, possessing various and manifold forms through the surging waves of radiant gnosis.
Through the power of the application of meditation and by the observance of the commitments,
such a form is attained that cannot even be described by the Victors.
Where there is neither body, speech, nor mind, but that supreme, all-pervading state— there,
by the power of the oral tradition, one's own true nature is manifested.
"Aho! How truly wondrous! Aho! How peaceful and beyond the senses! Aho! How supremely profound is Buddhahood, the highest state!
Thus it is said: "Aho, Vajra! Aho, Vajra! Aho, the teaching of the Vajra!"
"Where there is no body, speech, or mind, there form is clearly perceived.
Thus it was also said by the Venerable Master:
"There is no solidity in your body, nor is there flesh, bone, or blood."
You have displayed a body in the sky like a rainbow.
"There is no disease nor impurity in your body, nor is there the occurrence of hunger and thirst;
yet, for the sake of conforming to the world, you have demonstrated worldly activity. Thus it is said in the *Sarvakalpasamuccaya*:
"Having grasped the pure heart, through the visualization of the vajra-body, he has obtained the vajra-body which is firm, essential, and indestructible. Thus it is said:
"Equal to space, stainless, possessing supreme form, bodiless, and without characteristics—such is the daughter of Prajñā."
"O ocean of most profound qualities, O compassionate one, place your incomparable hand upon my head!
Thus ends the eighth chapter, "The Severing of Doubts Concerning the Integration into the Realm of Non-abiding Nirvāṇa. 8.
9. The ninth chapter:
"By sealing the cause with the effect, and by sealing the effect with the cause, one contemplates [the relationship]; otherwise, even in ten million eons, realization will not arise. Thus it is said.
"Vajrasattva, the great king, should be exhorted again and again. Thus,
having cast off the stretching out of the feet— that is, having abandoned the basket of saṃsāra—
one should accomplish the supreme Vajrasattva with a mind constantly applied.
"Having diligently abandoned remorse, sloth, torpor, and the like, otherwise there would be no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of eons. Thus it is said.
Those who abide here in the state of a monk, as well as those men who are devoted to logic (*tarka*), [should act accordingly].
"But for those who abide in the state of old age, one should not teach the reality.
Thus, O Great Hero, knowledge devoid of skillful means and even the training were taught for the sake of the Śrāvakas' entry [into the path].
One should indeed resort to them.
The *Mūlasūtra* also says:
"Those devoid of wisdom desire the ten paths of wholesome action. O monk, do not train in the Śrāvaka vehicle; train therein in the conduct of awakening.
"Practice the conduct of awakening toward the qualities of a Buddha; this will become the cause for you to become a Self-Existent One.
[Objection: "Through difficult and intense observances, the body withers and becomes miserable;
from misery the mind is distracted, and through distraction, success is otherwise [prevented]."
The *Mūlasūtra* also says:
"One who practices with difficult and intense observances does not attain success;
however, one who practices while enjoying all sensual pleasures attains success quickly."
Passion, hatred, and delusion— these three,
when improperly engaged, truly turn into poison if they are indulged in an unwholesome manner.
"Furthermore, they attain immortality when consumed with nectar. Thus,
by that which binds the dull-witted, the wise man is liberated.
Through the non-conceptualization of awakening, all this is seen as erroneous.
"By those very things through which the deluded are bound and destroyed in the vicinity of Raurava, they are indeed liberated through the power of wisdom. Thus it is said.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme universe in its entirety.
The *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
Always abiding in the supreme, most delightful secret, which is the self of all,
the glorious Vajrasattva arises as bliss, consisting of all Buddhas.
It is adorned with the great divine jewel-net of the Tathāgatas and so forth;
it is radiant, spread with a canopy from which bells are suspended.
One should perform the vajra song and the worship with the miraculous display of singing and instrumental music,
as well as through the application of flowers, incense, and so forth, and likewise with lamps, perfumes, and the like.
They accomplish the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* in their abodes or, alternatively, in gardens and other such places.
Having first placed the seat there, which provides the pleasure born of a soft touch and is covered with a cloth of the universal lotus— that indeed is the seat of total purity.
The union of all Buddhas, the miraculous manifestation of the Lord of Yoga— indeed,
it is there that they manifest in the form of Śrī Vajrasattva.
Whether consisting of all the elements or likewise consisting of the root of life,
one should set in motion the seals of accomplishment through the faces of one's own tutelary deity.
One should fashion the insignia-seal (cinhamudrā), whether it be cast, forged, refined, or beautifully painted, and featuring various distinct reflections.
Then, one should indeed place all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) upon those seats according to their respective locations.
One should [visualize] a square mandala with four doors, adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*),
and join the vajra, jewel, lotus, and so forth with the door-keepers.
One should fashion the circle of the Gaṇas, with women well-adorned facing their respective presiding deities, made auspicious by the marks of their own mudrās.
It is square, with four gates adorned by four archways,
provided with four boundary lines, and beautified by eight pillars.
Adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, decorated with bands,
garlands, and wreaths, beautified by bells and banners, and embellished with chowries and other ornaments.
With the corners marked by half-moons and vajras at the junctions of the doors and projections,
it is beautifully adorned with various cloths such as the *patākā*, *kramaśīrṣa*, and others.
While enjoying all the offerings of the goddesses as one pleases,
one should worship one's own self through the yoga of one's chosen deity.
One is honored through moderate application and by the bliss of all yoga;
however, one attains accomplishment by relishing it with excessive application.
By this elixir of bliss, which is the very self of all Buddhas, one shall attain the sublime happiness of longevity, youth, health, and well-being as Śrī Vajrasattva.
The great body of all Buddhas, the eloquence of all Buddhas,
the great mind of all Buddhas, the great festival of all Buddhas.
The great king of all Buddhas, the sovereign lord of all Vajra-holders,
the lord of all world-protectors, the sovereign lord of all jewels.
"Delighting with them, he goes toward rebirth;
indeed, as he proceeds, he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) who has attained the great siddhi of all goddesses. Thus it is said.
"Whether daily, monthly, or likewise annually, or according to one's specific commitment, one should perform the Buddha-saṃvara dance;
whether standing, sitting, walking, or remaining as one is."
Whether exulting or speaking, wherever and however one may do so;
Whatever sense faculty should enter the path, that very one, by its own nature,
through the yoga of non-concentration, should carry forth the essence of all Buddhas.
Equal to space, having the form of space, like a boundless ocean;
passion is the method of phenomena, hatred is its manifestation, and it is the expansion of play.
And the mere object is grasped for the sake of instructing the disciple;
how could the teaching on passion be tolerated if it were to speak of future births?

The ninth chapter, the Investigation of Doubts concerning the Melāvana—the elaboration of the awakening to the Dharma-source through the conduct of a Bodhisattva—according to the method of the *Śrīsarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. 9.
10. The Tenth Chapter:
This compendium of meditative concentration is to be accomplished in great forest regions, on mountains adorned with fruits, flowers, and the like, or in solitary places.
"Always enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure, one who desires knowledge [attains it].
Thus, by means of the very nature of the vajras of body, speech, and mind, the cultivation of body, speech, and mind must be performed; through that, swift accomplishment is attained.
One should cause a great image to be made, resembling white in color, wearing a crown of matted locks, and entirely conforming to the rules of the mantra-vow according to the prescribed ritual.
Having taken a sixteen-year-old girl, adorned with all ornaments,
possessing a beautiful face and large eyes, one should obtain her and practice the vow of the vidyā.
One should meditate upon her with the enjoyment of Locanā’s feet and the vajra symbols;
she who is skilled in the application of mudrās and mantras, and well-trained in the mantra-tantras.
One who observes the great vow should make the consort a Tathāgata-consort established in the enlightenment of the Buddha;
the practitioner of the great vow should perform the secret worship during the four sessions.
One should undertake all food and edibles consisting of bulbs, roots, and fruits;
in this way, one will quickly become a Buddha, a Lord who is an ocean of great wisdom.
Within six months alone, he shall attain all of that; there is no doubt in this matter.
The practitioner, firm in resolve, should wander daily for alms in the forest.
Terrified by fear, they offer them food adorned with divine [substances].
If one who is of the nature of vajra should transgress, the indestructible syllable (vajrākṣara) would meet its destruction.
"Having obtained a goddess, a nāginī, a great yakṣiṇī, an asurī, or even a human woman,
the observance of the vidyā-vow, which is served by the wisdom of the three vajras, should be performed. Thus, through the union of the two organs, the procedure for exertion occurs within.
The mind of joy in the sage’s accomplishment is known as "great bliss."
The tenth chapter: The Resolution of Doubts Concerning the Integration of the Practice Free from Conceptual Elaboration.
11. The eleventh chapter:
This compendium of meditations should be practiced in secluded mountains, by rivers and springs, and even in places such as cremation grounds.
The knower of reality should always avoid ritual applications and the like in their conventional sense;
except for the ego-identification with Vajrasattva, he should not perform anything else.
Even the preparatory applications are not perceived once one is established in pure reality,
as long as that is being scrutinized through the application of the state of selflessness.
For one who abides in the state of selflessness and is endowed with divine means,
whatever is enjoined in the ritual manuals is accomplished without deliberation.
Through the power of the yoga of meditation,
all that which constitutes the characteristics of accomplishment, whatever it may be, manifests spontaneously in a mere instant.
To perceive internal phenomena such as form and so forth is called *vipaśyanā* (insight);
to conceptualize them according to their respective order, such as Akṣobhya and the others, becomes *śamatha* (calm abiding).
"Because these two lack intrinsic nature, they are designated as the tranquility of suchness;
within the maṇḍala of suchness, the yogin should cause all Buddhas to enter. Thus it is said:
"In the great and terrible fire of nirvāṇa, one is not released even as ashes."
Therein no reality exists, nor sense objects, nor elements.
When the hero is free from conceptual construction, having abandoned worldly stability, he performs all activities; at that time, the Buddhas behold him.
One whose doubts are severed in every respect should move about with skillful means like a child;
when the yogi is free from mental effort, then all prosperities rain down.
For those possessed of every sin and firmly established in the veil of delusion,
the unerring accomplishments are attained within six months through the practice of the madman’s vow.
One shall personally behold all the Buddhas and be fulfilled by all desires;
there is neither exhaustion nor diminution, and one’s body and lifespan arise according to one's own wish.
One attains unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment without effort;
even those who are intent upon the enjoyment of all desires achieve success without exertion.
Whether walking, standing, or sitting, one should always proceed with profound words;
for this is the constant characteristic of yogins due to their skill in luminous gnosis.
By this yoga of meditation, the jewel of the mind becomes firm;
and the Buddhas, established in awakening, bestow their empowerment.
Having thus become established,
the wise one, intent on cultivation, should meditate with a concentrated mind until the consciousness becomes weary.
But when weary, one may wander about afterwards, acting as one pleases;
with eyes slightly opened, one should contemplate vast awakening.
Laughing and talking, sometimes standing still and sometimes moving about, he should carry out his activities.
But one whose mind is intent on cultivation should act in such a way that weariness does not arise.
Thus, for the mantra-practitioner who is endowed with such concentration and free from conceptual construction,
the unsurpassed state is accomplished by transcending the limitations of time.
[It is characterized by] a subtle form, a light touch, and the attainment of all-pervadingness.
"Clarity, stability, and mastery extending to the limit of all desires"—thus [it is said].
Having attained the supreme gnosis of awakening, one beholds the Buddha of radiant splendor;
and one quickly perceives oneself as the Buddha’s enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
He sees him being constantly worshipped by the great beings of the three realms,
as well as by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, with the five qualities of sensual pleasure.
He constantly beholds the worshiped Vajrasattva, the great image arising from vast primordial wisdom, and the highly renowned Vajradharma.
The one of great renown, the Secret Vajra, beholds his own form in a dream;
the Great Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajra-holders bow down before him.
They will see such dreams that bestow the accomplishments of body, speech, and mind,
as well as delightful celestial maidens adorned with every ornament.
Seeing a boy or a girl, he attains accomplishment;
he certainly beholds all the Buddhas residing in the realms of the ten directions.
With a joyful mind and soul, they give the delightful treasury of Dharma—
the body that has entered the wheel of Dharma and is surrounded by all sentient beings.
"One established in the vajra of meditative concentration beholds [it] at the time of yoga. And:
"Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything to be added;
reality is to be seen as it truly is; he who sees reality is liberated."
And it is said in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:
"The Buddha does not pass into parinirvāṇa, nor does the Dharma decline;
for the sake of maturing sentient beings, he manifests parinirvāṇa."
It is also said in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*: "Indeed, nothing whatsoever is produced here by conditions, nor is anything ceased;
it is only the imagined conditions themselves that are produced and cease."
Therefore it has been said:
"By whatever state of being the minds of men are joined,
they attain the nature of that very thing, just like a multiform gem."
Arising is that which is conventional truth, while death indeed is ultimate truth;
he who, through the guru’s compassion, comes to know these two stages shall become a Buddha.
The entry into the non-duality of the two truths is indeed without distinction, even though it takes the form of non-annihilation;
it is understood that there is only oneness between these two, by which one is liberated.
Just as someone who might fall from the summit of the king of mountains would not wish for the fall yet still falls,
so too one who has received instruction through the grace of the Guru may not wish for liberation, yet he is liberated nonetheless.

Having reflected upon the lack of capacity among beings to realize the ultimate truth, and observing the world as being like a lamp’s spark rendered feeble by the breaking of the waves of a surging ocean,
I have composed this treatise, gathering here whatever fragments I could find.
For those who are fortunate enough to be afraid of conventional truth, there would be no stain.
The eleventh chapter: The Severing of Doubts Concerning the Integration of the Practice of Absolute Non-proliferation.
This Lamp for the Compendium of Practices is completed.
This is the work of the great master, the venerable Āryadeva.
